This miscellaneous appeal has been preferred by appellant/non- applicant 2-The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd., challenging the award dated 09.12.2014 passed by Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Panna in MACC No.17/2013 whereby in the claim petition filed by respondents 1- Oriental Insurance Company Limited vs Smt. sentences.text:
Learned Counsel for the appellant/insurer submits that the offending vehicle bearing no.
MP35-T-0450 is a transport vehicle (known as Max-Cab) having seating capacity of 7+1, was being driven by non- applicant 1-Ashish Kumar Sharma (who is owner also), without requisite permit and valid license to drive the transport vehicle.
He submits that holding the non-transport LMV license to be valid, MACT erred in passing the impugned award and has not given any weightage to the registration number of the vehicle.
He submits that the letter 'T' mentioned in the registration number denotes that it was a transport vehicle and could be plied only upon having valid permit.
In support of his submissions, learned Counsel placed reliance on the decision in the case of National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Challa Bharathamma and others - 4 - (2004) 8 SCC 517.

entities.text: National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Challa Bharathamma and others - 4 - (2004) 8 SCC 517

sentences.text: With these submissions he prays for admitting/ allowing this miscellaneous appeal.

5. Learned counsel(s) appearing for respondents 1-6 (claimants and owner of vehicle) supports the impugned award and prays for dismissal of the miscellaneous appeal, with the submissions that there is no material available on record to hold that the offending vehicle was a transport vehicle.

They submit that in view of decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Mukund Dewangan vs.
Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. (2017) 14 SCC 663, even if the driver was having non- transport LMV license, having no endorsement about the transport vehicle, still the insurance company is liable to make payment of award.

sentences.text: They also submit that in absence of any evidence adduced by the insurance company to the effect that the vehicle was being driven without any permit, Tribunal has not committed any illegality in passing the impugned award.

6. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record.
7.
Upon perusal of record, it is clear that on the date of accident, non- applicant 1-Ashish Kumar Sharma was having a non-transport LMV license (Ex.D/2).

In the case of Mukund Dewangan (Supra) Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as under.
- 5 - "59.
Section 10 of the Act requires a driver to hold a licence with respect to the class of vehicles and not with respect to the type of vehicles.
In one class of vehicles, there may be different kinds of vehicles.
If they fall in the same class of vehicles, no separate endorsement is required to drive such vehicles.
As light motor vehicle includes transport vehicle also, a holder of light motor vehicle licence can drive all the vehicles of the class including transport vehicles.
It was pre-amended position as well the post-amended position of Form 4 as amended on 28-3-2001.

Even otherwise the forms never intended to exclude transport vehicles from the category of "light motor vehicles"
and for light motor vehicle, the validity period of such licence hold good and apply for the transport vehicle of such class also and the expression in Section 10(2)(e) of the Act "Transport Vehicle" would include medium goods vehicle, medium passenger motor vehicle, heavy goods vehicle, heavy passenger motor vehicle which earlier found place in Sections 10(2)(e) to (h) and our conclusion is fortified by the syllabus and rules which we have discussed.
60.

Thus, we answer the questions which are referred to us thus:
60.1. "Light motor vehicle" as defined in Section 2(21) of the Act would include a transport vehicle as per the weight prescribed in Section 2(21) read with Sections 2(15) and 2(48).
Such transport vehicles are not excluded from the definition of the light motor vehicle by virtue of Amendment Act 54 of 1994.

60.2. A transport vehicle and omnibus, the gross vehicle weight of either of which does not exceed 7500 kg would be a light motor vehicle and also motor car or tractor or a roadroller, "unladen weight" of which does not exceed 7500 kg and holder of a driving licence to drive class of "light motor vehicle"as provided in Section 10(2)(d) is competent to drive a transport vehicle or omnibus, the gross vehicle weight of which does not exceed 7500 kg or a motor car or tractor or roadroller, the "unladen weight"
of which does not exceed 7500 kg.
That is to say, no separate endorsement on the licence is required to drive a transport vehicle of light motor vehicle class as enumerated above.
A licence - 6 - issued under Section 10(2)(d) continues to be valid after Amendment Act 54 of 1994 and 28-3-2001 in the form.

The effect of the amendment made by virtue of Act 54 of 1994 w.e.f. 14-11-1994 while substituting clauses (e) to (h) of Section 10(2) which contained "medium goods vehicle" in Section 10(2)(e), "medium passenger motor vehicle" in Section 10(2)(f), "heavy goods vehicle" in Section 10(2)(g) and "heavy passenger motor vehicle" in Section 10(2)(h) with expression "transport vehicle" as substituted in Section 10(2)(e) related only to the aforesaid substituted classes only.
It does not exclude transport vehicle, from the purview of Section 10(2)(d) and Section 2(41) of the Act i.e. light motor vehicle.

60.4. The effect of amendment of Form 4 by insertion of "transport vehicle"
is related only to the categories which were substituted in the year 1994 and the procedure to obtain driving licence for transport vehicle of class of "light motor vehicle" continues to be the same as it was and has not been changed and there is no requirement to obtain separate endorsement to drive Oriental Insurance Company Limited vs Smt. 8.

In the present case it is undisputed fact that non-applicant 1 was having valid LMV license to drive non-transport vehicle, therefore, in view of decision in the case of Mukund Dewangan (Supra),
it cannot be said that there being breach of insurance policy, the insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation.
Hence, on this ground MACT does not appear to have committed any illegality in holding the insurance company to be liable to pay the awarded amount.

9. So far as the question of possessing valid permit is concerned, in the instant case, for the reasons best known to the appellant/insurance company, no evidence has been adduced to prove the alleged breach of - 7 - conditions of the policy, in absence of which findings recorded by MACT to the effect that offending vehicle was being plied by the non-applicant 1-Ashish Kumar Sharma for his personal use, cannot be said to be illegal or unsustainable.

10. Even otherwise, in the instant case, non-applicant 1-owner/driver has examined himself i.e.
Ashish Kumar Sharma (NAW-1), who has placed on record Certificate of Registration (Ex.D/1c);
Driving License (Ex.D/2c); Policy (Ex.D/3c) and Fitness certificate (Ex.D/4c), but the non-applicant 2/insurer has neither adduced any evidence regarding breach of any of the conditions of the policy nor has put any question to Ashish Kumar Sharma (NAW-1) in his cross-examination that he had no permit of the vehicle on the date of accident.
11.

It is well settled that in case of any plea of breach of conditions of policy, the same is required to be proved by the insurance company itself by adducing cogent and admissible evidence, in absence of which it cannot be said that the offending vehicle was being driven in breach of any of the conditions of insurance policy.

12. Hon'ble Supreme Court has, in the case of FAHIM AHMAD & ORS. Vs. UNITED INDIA INSURANCE CO. LTD. & ORS. 2014 ACJ 1254 =AIR 2014 SC 2187, held as under :
- 8 - "8.

sentences.text: Although the plea of breach of the conditions of policy was raised before the Tribunal, yet neither any issue was framed nor any evidence led to prove the same.
In our opinion, it was mandatory for respondent No. 1-lnsurance Company not only to plead the said breach, but also substantiate the same by adducing positive evidence in respect of the same.
In the absence of any such evidence, it cannot be presumed that there was breach of the conditions of policy."

Further, in the case of NARCHINVA V. KAMAT AND ANOTHER VERSUS ALFREDO ANTONIO DEO MARTINS AND OTHERS 1985 ACJ 397 = AIR 1985 SC 1281, Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as under :
"14.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The last question is whether he had a valid driving licence.
The High Court has not recorded a clear cut finding on this point.
The finding of the Tribunal is more evasive than the one by the High Court.
Mr. Sharma did not dispute that the. second appellant had a driving licence.

His grievance is that he having failed to produce the same when called upon to do so in the cross- examination, an adverse inference be drawn against him that he did not have a valid licence to drive a pick-up van.
The submission fails to carry conviction with us.
The burden to prove that there was breach of the contract of insurance was squarely placed on the shoulders of the insurance company.
It could not be said to have been discharged by it by a mere question in cross-examination.
The second appellant was under no obligation to furnish evidence so as to enable the insurance company to wriggle out its liability under the contract of insurance.
Further the R.T.A. which issues the driving licence keeps a record of the licences issued and renewed by it.
The insurance company could have got the evidence produced to substantiate his allegation.
Applying the test who would fail if no evidence is led, the obvious answer is the insurance company.

15. To sum up the insurance company failed to prove that there was a breach of the term of the contract of insurance as evidenced by the policy of insurance on the ground that the driver who was driving the vehicle at the relevant time did not have a valid driving licence.

Once the insurance company failed to prove that aspect, its liability under the contract of insurance remains intact and unhampered and it was bound to satisfy the award under the comprehens- ive policy of insurance."

14. In view of the aforesaid settled legal position it is clear that in absence of apparent breach of policy, entire burden is on the insurer to adduce positive evidence to prove breach of conditions of the policy by getting produced evidence from the office of concerning R.T.A. and in - 9 - absence of any evidence adduced by the appellant/insurance company, it cannot be said that MACT has committed any illegality in passing the impugned award.
15. Resultantly, this Miscellaneous Appeal fails and is hereby dismissed at its admission stage itself.
16. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed off.
